title: Postpartum Hemorrhage: Bleeding Can Turn Critical Fast
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Heavy or rapidly increasing postpartum bleeding with tachycardia, hypotension, dizziness, pallor, uterine atony, or worsening weakness requires immediate hemorrhage response. Do not wait for a dramatic blood-pressure drop before escalating.
recognize: Heavy/gushing bleeding, large clots, boggy uterus, tachycardia, pallor, dizziness, weakness, confusion, or falling BP are danger cues.
Hemorrhage can occur immediately after birth or later in the postpartum course.
priorities: Call for obstetric emergency help and follow the hemorrhage protocol.
Assess bleeding, uterine tone if within role, vital signs, perfusion, and IV access while ordered treatment is initiated.
assessMonitor: Trend quantified/estimated blood loss, uterine tone, fundal position, HR/BP, mental status, urine output, and response to uterotonics/fluids/blood products.
interventions: Support uterine massage and bladder emptying if authorized, maintain access, administer ordered uterotonics/fluids, and prepare for escalation/procedures.
medicationSafety: Uterotonic selection depends on contraindications such as hypertension or asthma; verify drug-specific safety rather than treating all uterotonics as interchangeable.
teaching: After discharge, heavy bleeding, faintness, racing heart, or rapidly worsening weakness requires urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Hemorrhage recognition and emergency escalation are licensed-nurse responsibilities; medication/procedure authority follows state and facility policy.
examTrap: Reassuring the patient because some lochia is expected while systemic hypovolemia is developing.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum bleeding is judged by the patient’s stability, not by whether bleeding is expected after birth.
sourceBasis: ACOG Postpartum Hemorrhage Practice Bulletin reaffirmed 2024 with 2025 update

title: Postpartum Preeclampsia: Delivery Does Not End the Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: New severe headache, visual change, dyspnea, upper-abdominal pain, marked hypertension, or neurologic symptoms after delivery may indicate postpartum preeclampsia and require urgent evaluation—even after a normotensive pregnancy.
recognize: Postpartum preeclampsia can present after discharge and may occur after previously normal pregnancy blood pressures.
Headache unrelieved by usual measures, vision changes, dyspnea, or seizures are high-risk cues.
priorities: Confirm BP correctly and escalate concerning symptoms promptly.
Do not dismiss severe headache or dyspnea as normal postpartum fatigue.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, neurologic symptoms, vision, respiratory status, edema, urine output, and ordered laboratory findings.
interventions: Reduce stimulation/seizure risk as indicated, administer ordered antihypertensive or magnesium therapy where authorized, and monitor for toxicity.
medicationSafety: Magnesium sulfate requires respiratory, reflex, urine-output and toxicity monitoring; antihypertensive choice follows obstetric protocol.
teaching: Postpartum hypertension warning signs remain important for weeks after delivery; seek urgent care for severe headache, visual changes, breathing difficulty, or seizure.
delegationScope: Routine BP collection may be delegated with thresholds; interpretation and escalation of symptomatic hypertension remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Assuming preeclampsia cannot begin after the placenta is delivered.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum plus headache or vision change means check pressure and think preeclampsia.
sourceBasis: CDC Hear Her urgent maternal warning signs

title: Postpartum Endometritis: Fever Plus Uterine Symptoms Is Not Normal Recovery
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Postpartum fever, chills, uterine/abdominal tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, tachycardia, or systemic illness should trigger evaluation for endometritis or sepsis rather than being attributed to normal postpartum recovery.
recognize: Endometritis often appears within days after delivery but can occur later.
Fever with uterine tenderness or foul discharge is particularly concerning.
priorities: Escalate promptly and assess for sepsis.
Obtain ordered cultures/labs without delaying antibiotics when the patient is unstable.
assessMonitor: Monitor temperature, HR/BP, uterine/abdominal tenderness, lochia, incision/perineum, mental status, urine output, and response to antibiotics.
interventions: Administer ordered antibiotics/fluids and support sepsis protocol as indicated.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic therapy must match the obstetric infection plan and allergy history; monitor for C. difficile and drug reactions.
teaching: Fever, chills, worsening pelvic pain, or foul-smelling discharge after birth needs medical review.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; suspected postpartum infection with systemic change requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Treating postpartum fever as expected milk-coming-in discomfort without assessing uterine and systemic infection cues.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum fever plus uterine tenderness or foul lochia is infection until evaluated.

title: Postpartum VTE: One-Sided Leg Symptoms or Sudden Dyspnea Are Emergencies
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Postpartum hypercoagulability increases VTE risk. New unilateral leg swelling/pain, chest pain, unexplained tachycardia, hemoptysis, syncope, or sudden dyspnea requires urgent evaluation for DVT/PE.
recognize: A swollen, painful, warm unilateral leg is concerning for DVT.
Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or unexplained tachycardia may indicate PE.
priorities: Do not massage a suspected DVT limb.
Escalate suspected PE immediately and support oxygenation/circulation as ordered.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory status, HR/BP, oxygen saturation, leg asymmetry/swelling, pain, mobility, and anticoagulant therapy when prescribed.
interventions: Maintain safety, limit unnecessary ambulation with suspected acute DVT until evaluated, and administer ordered anticoagulation where authorized.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant safety requires bleeding surveillance, medication reconciliation, and product-specific pregnancy/lactation considerations.
teaching: Urgent evaluation is needed for new one-sided leg swelling/pain or sudden breathing/chest symptoms after delivery.
delegationScope: Suspected VTE requires licensed assessment and escalation; anticoagulant administration follows local scope/policy.
examTrap: Massaging a painful swollen calf to improve circulation.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum clot risk is real—one-sided leg symptoms or sudden dyspnea are not watch-and-wait findings.
sourceBasis: CDC Hear Her urgent maternal warning signs
Current U.S. obstetric VTE safety principles

title: Cesarean and Perineal Wound Recovery: Separate Healing From Infection or Hematoma
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Postpartum incision or perineal pain should gradually improve. Increasing redness, drainage, separation, fever, severe focal pressure/pain, expanding swelling, or systemic illness requires evaluation for infection, dehiscence, or hematoma.
recognize: Expected tenderness should trend down rather than intensify.
Severe perineal pain with swelling and limited visible bleeding can indicate hematoma.
priorities: Inspect wound/perineum per role and assess pain trend, fever, drainage, odor, swelling, and function.
Escalate wound separation, rapidly increasing pain/swelling, or systemic deterioration.
assessMonitor: Monitor incision/perineum, temperature, pain, mobility, urination, bowel function, and drainage.
interventions: Provide ordered wound/perineal care, hygiene, pain control, and pressure-reduction measures.
medicationSafety: Analgesics can mask worsening symptoms; reassess function and tissue findings rather than documenting pain relief alone.
teaching: Report worsening pain, fever, foul drainage, opening of the incision, or rapidly enlarging swelling.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene/support may be delegated; abnormal wound findings require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Assuming severe perineal pain is normal because the visible bleeding is limited.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum wounds should improve—worsening pain, swelling, drainage, or separation is a cue to escalate.
sourceBasis: ACOG postpartum recovery and warning-sign resources

title: Postpartum Urinary Retention: A Full Bladder Can Worsen Recovery
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Failure to void, small frequent voids, suprapubic fullness, increasing uterine displacement, or excessive residual urine after birth may indicate postpartum urinary retention and can worsen discomfort, bleeding, or infection risk.
recognize: Epidural/spinal anesthesia, perineal trauma, prolonged labor, edema, and catheter exposure can contribute.
A distended bladder can displace the uterus and interfere with effective contraction.
priorities: Track timely voiding and symptoms after catheter removal/birth.
Escalate inability to void, painful distention, or significant residual per protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor voiding pattern, bladder distention, urine output, dysuria, uterine position/bleeding context, and catheter history.
interventions: Promote privacy, mobility, hydration within plan, and catheterization per order/protocol when required.
medicationSafety: Review anticholinergic/opioid medications that may worsen retention.
redFlags: Unable to void with painful distention
Low urine output with systemic instability
teaching: Report inability to urinate, severe bladder pressure, or persistent burning/pain.
delegationScope: Intake/output collection may be delegated; retention assessment and catheter decisions require licensed oversight and local policy.
examTrap: Documenting repeated tiny voids as adequate output without assessing for overflow retention.
oneLinePearl: Frequent small voids can still mean a very full postpartum bladder.

title: Lactational Mastitis: Treat Inflammation and Watch for Abscess
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Localized breast pain/redness with systemic symptoms may represent mastitis. Support milk removal/feeding as clinically appropriate, avoid aggressive breast trauma, and escalate worsening systemic illness, persistent focal mass, or failure to improve for abscess evaluation.
recognize: Breast tenderness, erythema, warmth, fever, chills, and malaise can occur.
Persistent fluctuant mass or failure to improve raises concern for abscess.
priorities: Assess severity, hydration, feeding/milk-removal pattern, and systemic illness.
Escalate sepsis signs or suspected abscess.
assessMonitor: Monitor fever, pain, erythema extent, breast mass, feeding tolerance, hydration, and response to treatment.
interventions: Support rest, hydration, comfortable feeding/milk removal, cold/comfort measures, and prescribed antibiotics when bacterial mastitis is diagnosed.
medicationSafety: Verify lactation compatibility and allergy history for prescribed antibiotics/analgesics.
teaching: Seek follow-up if symptoms worsen or do not improve; avoid forceful massage of inflamed tissue.
delegationScope: Feeding support may be shared within competency; systemic deterioration or suspected abscess requires licensed/provider evaluation.
examTrap: Telling the patient to stop breastfeeding automatically whenever mastitis is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Mastitis care supports the breast and the patient—worsening systemic illness or a persistent mass needs escalation.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. lactational mastitis practice principles

title: Postpartum Depression: Screen, Listen, Escalate Safety Concerns
clientNeeds: Psychosocial Integrity
Health Promotion and Maintenance
bottomLine: Persistent sadness, anxiety, anhedonia, guilt, impaired bonding/function, or inability to care for self/baby warrants evaluation for postpartum depression. Suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby require immediate safety escalation.
recognize: Symptoms that persist, worsen, or significantly impair function exceed expected transient postpartum emotional lability.
Risk can emerge after discharge and throughout the postpartum year.
priorities: Ask directly about suicidal ideation and thoughts of harming the infant when indicated.
Escalate immediate safety risk and connect the patient with urgent mental-health care.
assessMonitor: Monitor mood, anxiety, sleep beyond infant-related disruption, function, bonding, appetite, support, substance use, and safety.
interventions: Use validated screening per program, reinforce follow-up, mobilize support, and maintain safety precautions when needed.
medicationSafety: Psychotropic selection during lactation requires individualized prescriber review; do not advise abrupt antidepressant discontinuation.
teaching: Postpartum depression is treatable; severe symptoms or safety thoughts need immediate help.
delegationScope: Screen administration may be delegated by protocol; interpretation, suicide-risk assessment, and escalation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Calling severe persistent depression 'baby blues' because the patient recently delivered.
oneLinePearl: Duration, severity, function, and safety separate transient blues from dangerous postpartum depression.
sourceBasis: CDC Hear Her maternal warning signs

title: Postpartum Psychosis: Psychiatric Emergency, Not Severe Baby Blues
clientNeeds: Psychosocial Integrity
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: New hallucinations, delusions, severe disorganization, mania, profound agitation, bizarre beliefs about the infant, or rapidly fluctuating behavior postpartum may represent postpartum psychosis and require emergency psychiatric evaluation and continuous safety protection.
recognize: Psychosis can emerge rapidly after birth and may include little sleep, agitation, confusion, paranoia, delusions, or hallucinations.
Risk of suicide or infant harm can be substantial.
priorities: Do not leave a high-risk patient alone with the infant.
Activate emergency psychiatric/safety response and remove immediate hazards.
assessMonitor: Monitor behavior, orientation, psychotic symptoms, sleep, agitation, suicidal/infanticidal thoughts, and response to emergency treatment.
interventions: Maintain calm supervision, protect patient/infant, reduce stimulation, and facilitate urgent psychiatric care.
medicationSafety: Emergency psychiatric medications require monitoring for sedation, hypotension, movement disorders, and lactation considerations as ordered.
teaching: Families should treat sudden bizarre behavior, hallucinations, or severe confusion after birth as an emergency.
delegationScope: Safety observation may be assigned only with clear parameters; psychiatric risk assessment and disposition require licensed/qualified clinicians.
examTrap: Using routine postpartum reassurance for a patient describing voices telling her the baby is evil.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency because reality testing—and safety—can disappear quickly.

title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: Dyspnea Is Not Always Normal Postpartum Fatigue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, chest discomfort, palpitations, marked edema, syncope, or unexplained tachycardia postpartum may signal heart failure/peripartum cardiomyopathy and should not be dismissed as normal recovery.
recognize: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pulmonary crackles, new hypoxemia, and disproportionate edema are concerning.
Symptoms overlap with normal postpartum fatigue, making trend and severity important.
priorities: Assess ABCs and escalate respiratory or circulatory compromise immediately.
Differentiate new cardiopulmonary symptoms from routine postpartum discomfort through focused assessment.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory effort, SpO2, HR/BP, lung sounds, edema, urine output, weight trend, and response to ordered heart-failure therapy.
interventions: Position upright, provide ordered oxygen/monitoring, conserve activity, and prepare for cardiac evaluation.
medicationSafety: Heart-failure medication choices postpartum must consider hemodynamics, renal function, potassium, and lactation when applicable.
teaching: Seek urgent care for new severe shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, or rapidly worsening swelling after pregnancy.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated with thresholds; new cardiopulmonary deterioration requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Attributing new orthopnea and tachycardia to sleep deprivation after delivery.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum dyspnea that is new, progressive, or positional deserves a heart-and-lung evaluation.
sourceBasis: CDC Hear Her urgent maternal warning signs
Current U.S. peripartum cardiomyopathy safety principles
